{{Short description|Term from the theory of normed spaces}}
{{other uses|Schur's lemma (disambiguation)}}In [[mathematics]], '''Schur's property''', named after [[Issai Schur]], is the property of [[normed vector space|normed space]]s that is satisfied precisely if [[weak topology|weak convergence]] of '''sequences''' entails convergence in norm.

==Motivation==
When we are working in a normed space ''X'' and we have a sequence <math>(x_{n})</math> that converges weakly to <math>x</math>, then a natural question arises. Does the sequence converge in perhaps a more desirable manner? If so, does the sequence converge to <math>x</math> in norm? A canonical example of this property, and commonly used to illustrate the Schur property, is the <math>\ell_1</math> [[sequence space]].

==Definition==
Suppose that we have a normed space <math>(X, \|\cdot\|)</math>, <math>x</math> an arbitrary member of <math>X</math>, and <math>(x_{n})</math> an arbitrary sequence in the space. We say that <math>X</math> has '''Schur's property''' if <math>(x_{n})</math> converging weakly to <math>x</math> implies that <math>\lim_{n\to\infty} \Vert x_n - x\Vert = 0 </math>. In other words, the weak and strong topologies share the same convergent sequences. Note however that weak and strong topologies are always distinct in infinite-dimensional space.

==Examples==
{{Expand section|date=February 2021}}
The space ''ℓ<sup>1</sup>'' of sequences whose series is absolutely convergent has the Schur property.

==Name==
This property was named after the early 20th century mathematician [[Issai Schur]] who showed that ''ℓ<sup>1</sup>'' had the above property in his 1921 paper.<ref>J. Schur, "Über lineare Transformationen in der Theorie der unendlichen Reihen", '' Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik'', '''151''' (1921) pp. 79-111</ref>
